facts.claim: "Humankind" was released as a single on June 21, 2024, on Miserable Music Group.
The song is credited to David Kushner, Sean Douglas, Jeremy Dussolliet and Tim Sommers as writers, with One Love as producer.
It runs 3:03 and appears as a track on Kushner's debut studio album The Dichotomy, released August 30, 2024.
Kushner announced The Dichotomy alongside the release of the "Humankind" single and music video.
The song draws on Kushner's personal experience of church trauma.
Kushner said he wanted to depict humankind's struggle between light and darkness. He called it something he feels daily and said there are always two sides to everything.
The music video opens with Kushner sitting alone in a dilapidated church.
A "Humankind (Reimagined)" release from 2024 includes cinematic, slowed + reverb, sped up and instrumental versions.
Kushner was born David Alan Kushner II on September 6, 2000, in Chicago, Illinois. He is a self-taught guitarist whose single "Miserable Man" went viral on TikTok in 2022.
His earlier single "Daylight" (April 14, 2023) was the lead single from The Dichotomy, was produced by Rob Kirwan, and peaked at number two on the UK Singles Chart.

research.lineage: The song sits in the folk-pop and indie-folk singer-songwriter tradition, with gospel and church-trauma themes and TikTok-driven reach; one source lists Hozier, The Lumineers and Bon Iver as influences.

draft:
The devil in **Humankind** isn't waiting at a crossroads. He's in church on a Sunday morning with his hands in the air, and he "blew his paycheck on the plate that they were passing." David Kushner's opening verse makes him the most generous man in the room. He has the spirit, he testifies in the light, he dresses well. The only flaw the song lets slip is that he was heartless in prayer. That's the sharpest move here: the hypocrite doesn't look like a villain. He looks like the man everyone admires.

The song comes out of Kushner's own experience of church trauma, and the chorus sounds like someone who walked in thirsty: "I was looking for living water / You just let me drown." Living water is scripture's promise of a faith that keeps you alive, and Kushner turns it into the thing that pulled him under. The anger is real, but listen to the vocabulary: slaughtered, heavens, sinners, tradition. He can't describe what hurt him without the language it taught him. That's the grief under the bitterness. He still wants what he was promised.

The second verse widens the blame and quietly takes some of it on. Loving the ones who hurt us and hurting the ones we love is a "we" line, not a "you" line, and it keeps the song from becoming a sermon against sermons. Kushner said he wanted to show the struggle between light and darkness, something he feels every day, because there are always two sides to everything. Then the bridge drops the case entirely. He admits he's only human and asks someone to take his hand. After all that accusation, what's left is need.

The arrangement gathers the way a slow hymn gathers a congregation. A clean electric guitar picks out arpeggiated chords over a steady bass line, kick and snare step in, a synth pad fills the space behind them, and the reverb gives everything room to hang. Kushner's voice is raspy and a little breathy, holding notes long rather than pushing them, and on the wordless "oh" refrains the harmonies stack up into something close to a choir. It's polished folk-pop with the gospel-haunted earnestness of the acts he counts as influences, Hozier, the Lumineers, Bon Iver.

Written with Sean Douglas, Jeremy Dussolliet and Tim Sommers and produced by One Love, it arrived as the announcement of his debut album, The Dichotomy, with a video that opens on Kushner alone in a dilapidated church. The album's title fits the song exactly.

What sticks is the split it leaves you holding: a chorus that lets you rage at the people who failed you, and a bridge that admits you still want someone to reach for.
